name: Fat burning zone
seoDesc: Fat burning zone: work out maximum heart rate (MHR) from the age. A free sports calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Fat burning zone calculator takes the numbers you enter and reports maximum heart rate (MHR) immediately. It is free to use, needs no account, and shows the working rather than just the answer. Think of it as a shortcut for a training session, a performance comparison or a competition result. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Fat burning zone calculator work?
sections.html:
The Fat burning zone calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports maximum heart rate (MHR) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the age.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A measured quantity, entered by default in years. The unit chip switches it to any of the 27 supported units.
  • A number, expressed in bpm.

sections.title: The formula behind the Fat burning zone calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Maximum heart rate (MHR)=220 − age
Maximum heart rate (MHR)=heart rate reserve (HRR) + resting heart rate (RHR)
Maximum heart rate (MHR)=(5 ÷ 3) × maximum heart rate 60
Maximum heart rate (MHR)=(5 ÷ 4) × maximum heart rate 80
Maximum heart rate (MHR)=maximum heart rate min55 + 55
Maximum heart rate min 35=maximum heart rate (MHR) − 35

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Age = 10 yrs. The calculator returns Maximum heart rate (MHR) = 219.9989, Maximum heart rate 60 = 132, Maximum heart rate 80 = 176 and Maximum heart rate min 35 = 185.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Maximum heart rate (MHR) = 219.9989, Maximum heart rate 60 = 132, Maximum heart rate 80 = 176 and Maximum heart rate min 35 = 185 should be roughly the size you expected from Age = 10 yrs.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Time, opening in years

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Fat burning zone calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Tracking progress across a training block
  • Planning a session around a target you already know
  • Comparing two athletes or two attempts fairly
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the age — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Fat burning zone calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns maximum heart rate (MHR), derived from the age. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Fat burning zone calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the age, which is 2 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter age in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Age opens in years and the chip beside it offers 27 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Maximum heart rate (MHR) = 219.9989. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Fat burning zone calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
